A_target.statement: The [[Definition:Hamiltonian Cycle Problem|Hamiltonian cycle problem]], of deciding whether a [[Definition:Graph (Graph Theory)|graph]] has a [[Definition:Hamiltonian Cycle|Hamiltonian cycle]], is [[Definition:NP-Hard|NP-hard]].

B_source.statement: The [[Definition:Vertex Cover Problem|vertex cover problem]], of deciding whether a [[Definition:Graph (Graph Theory)|graph]] $G$ has a [[Definition:Vertex Cover|vertex cover]] of size at most $k$, is [[Definition:NP-Hard|NP-hard]].

substitutions.the vertex cover instance: a graph together with a target cover size
substitutions.the gadget replacing each edge: a fixed subgraph traversable in exactly two ways
substitutions.the selector vertices: vertices whose number equals the target cover size

derived.a cover of the given size: a Hamiltonian cycle passing through the gadgets in the corresponding order
derived.the equivalence of the two instances: the constructed graph has a Hamiltonian cycle exactly when a cover of that size exists

object_map.reformulation: Encode the covering choice as the traversal direction through a gadget, turning a selection problem into a routing problem.

validity_conditions: The construction must be computable in polynomial time, so the gadget size and their number must be bounded by a polynomial in the original instance.
Each edge gadget admits exactly two traversal patterns, corresponding to which endpoint is chosen in the cover, which is what makes the correspondence exact.
Both directions of the equivalence must be checked: a cover yields a cycle and a cycle yields a cover, since hardness requires the instances to be genuinely equivalent.
proof_plan: Given an instance $\tuple {G, k}$ of vertex cover, build a graph $H$ with one gadget of $12$ vertices for each [[Definition:Edge of Graph|edge]] of $G$, and $k$ selector vertices $s_1, \ldots, s_k$.

For each vertex $u$ of $G$, chain the gadgets of the edges incident to $u$ into a path, and join both ends of the path to every selector.
Each gadget can be traversed in exactly three ways, corresponding to which endpoint(s) of its edge cover it.

Let $C$ be a cover with $\card C = k$.
Route the cycle from $s_i$ through the path of the $i$th vertex of $C$ to $s_{i + 1}$, visiting each gadget according to which endpoints lie in $C$.
This gives a [[Definition:Hamiltonian Cycle|Hamiltonian cycle]] in $H$.

Conversely, a Hamiltonian cycle in $H$ passes between consecutive selectors along exactly $k$ vertex paths.
The corresponding $k$ vertices cover every edge, as every gadget is visited.
As $H$ is built in polynomial time, the problem is [[Definition:NP-Hard|NP-hard]].
{{qed}}
